targetText:
The employés
themselves fixed the price and plundered at will the unhappy Hindus.
summary: Colonial plunder by commercial monopolies: the English East India Company plunders the Indian subcontinent.
explanation: Marx documents how European chartered trading monopolies, such as the English East India Company, wielded political conquest to establish private trade monopolies over essential goods (salt, opium, grain), generating vast fortunes through extortion and devastating famine among the Indian population.
context: Part VIII, Chapter 31: Genesis of the Industrial Capitalist

targetText:
The nations bragged cynically of every infamy that served
them as a means to capitalistic accumulation.
summary: Cynical celebration of colonial brutality: European states brag of atrocities that fuel capital accumulation.
explanation: Marx observes that with the rise of modern capitalism, bourgeois public opinion discarded all moral pretenses, openly boasting of imperialist piracy, treaty violations, and violent subjugation of colonized peoples because these actions expanded domestic capital accumulation.
context: Part VIII, Chapter 31: Genesis of the Industrial Capitalist

targetText:
The discovery of gold and silver in America, the extirpation,
enslavement and entombment in mines of the aboriginal population, the beginning
of the conquest and looting of the East Indies, the turning of Africa into
a warren for the commercial hunting of black-skins, signalised the rosy
dawn of the era of capitalist production. These idyllic proceedings are
the chief momenta of primitive accumulation.
summary: The birth of capitalism ("primitive accumulation") was built directly on Indigenous genocide, colonial plunder, and the transatlantic slave trade.
explanation: Marx refutes the bourgeois myth that capitalism arose from peaceful thrift, showing that European industrial wealth was accumulated through Indigenous dispossession in the Americas, colonial looting in India, and the enslavement of Africans.

targetText:
Those sober virtuosi of Protestantism, the Puritans of New England, in
1703, by decrees of their assembly set a premium of £40 on every
Indian scalp and every captured red-skin: in 1720 a premium of £100
on every scalp; in 1744, after Massachusetts-Bay had proclaimed a certain
tribe as rebels, the following prices: for a male scalp of 12 years and
upwards £100 (new currency), for a male prisoner £105, for
women and children prisoners £50, for scalps of women and children
£50.
summary: Settler-colonial primitive accumulation: colonial legislatures placed state bounties on the scalps and capture of Indigenous men, women, and children.
explanation: Marx documents how settler-colonial governments in North America used state-sanctioned racial terror and bounties to exterminate Indigenous nations and expropriate their land.

targetText:
Whilst the cotton industry introduced child-slavery in England,
it gave in the United States a stimulus to the transformation of the earlier,
more or less patriarchal slavery, into a system of commercial exploitation.
In fact, the veiled slavery of the wage workers in Europe needed, for its
pedestal, slavery pure and simple in the new world.
summary: European industrial wage-labor stood on the pedestal of racial chattel slavery in the Americas.
explanation: Marx shows that British textile mills and industrial capitalism depended directly on cotton produced by enslaved Black labor in the American South, linking anti-racist abolitionism to the emancipation of wage workers.

targetText: capital comes dripping from head to foot, from every pore, with blood and dirt.
summary: Capital entered the world soaked in blood and dirt from every pore.
explanation: Marx closes his survey of the colonial system, the national debt and the modern tax system with this image to stress that capitalist accumulation relied on state violence, plunder and slave trading.
context: The line summarises the historical argument that violence was the midwife of the new mode of production.
